105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and P: Game of Thrones, HBO's adaptation of George R. R. Martin's fantasy saga, enthralled the 2010s with its dynastic wars, political scheming, and willingness to kill off anyone. Its sprawling cast of flawed, morally compromised characters is a philosopher's playground: essays here ask whether Arya's revenge makes the show itself morally suspect, what Ned Stark's ruinous honor teaches about tragedy, where power really comes from, and how humor, disability, consent, and prophecy work in Westeros.
106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a: Peanuts is Charles Schulz's beloved comic strip, running from 1950 to 2000, about round-headed Charlie Brown, his beagle Snoopy, and a circle of children who talk like anxious adults. Beneath the jokes about kites and footballs lies real melancholy: essays here read the strip through existentialism, asking why Charlie's endless failures carry dignity, whether Linus's Great Pumpkin faith could ever be rational, what Lucy's cruelty owes to Kant, and how happiness, desire, and morality look from the sandbox.
107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Commo: Deadpool is Marvel's 'Merc with a Mouth,' a scarred, wisecracking, unkillable mercenary famous for cracking jokes about the comics, films, and audience watching him. His fourth-wall breaking makes him an unlikely philosopher: essays here ask whether stepping outside his own story is the examined life, whether an immortal can still find life worth living, what separates hero from villain from asshole, and how much violence and bad taste a character can carry and stay lovable.
109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond: Mr. Robot is the USA Network thriller (2015-2019) about Elliot Alderson, a brilliant, mentally fragile hacker drawn into fsociety's plot to erase the world's debt by destroying the financial giant E Corp. The show's blend of paranoia, technology, and political rage raises hard questions: essays here ask whether the hack was anarchist revolution or revenge, whether it can be justified by just war theory, what privacy means in a surveilled economy, and who really holds power in a world run by the grid.
111 - The Man in the High Castle and Phi: The Man in the High Castle, Philip K. Dick's novel and Amazon's series adaptation, imagines an America that lost World War II and is partitioned between Nazi and Japanese rule. The setting forces viewers to think the unthinkable: essays here ask whether resisting fascism counts as terrorism, why we end up rooting for Nazi characters, how architecture and propaganda shape belief, what keeps alternative memory alive under totalitarianism, and how close that dark timeline really is to ours.
112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Red: The Americans is the acclaimed FX spy drama (2013-2018) about two Soviet KGB officers living undercover in 1980s Washington as an ordinary married couple with American-born children. This book uses the show's central tension between marriage and politics to ask big questions about power: where the patriarchal family and the state came from, how husbands and wives struggle over money, work, and sex, what the classic social contract theorists got wrong about women and race, and how much has changed since 1960.
113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Expe: Jimi Hendrix (1942-1970) is widely held to be rock's greatest guitarist, transforming electric guitar in barely four years with records like Are You Experienced and his incendiary Woodstock rendition of the Star-Spangled Banner. Essays here treat his sound as serious thought: his burning guitar and feedback as Zen teaching, his antiwar noise as philosophy you feel in the body, his quest for freedom and love, whether his chaotic genius fits Kant's account of creativity, and how many 'Jimi' identities one life can hold.
114 - American Horror Story and Philosop: American Horror Story is FX's horror anthology (since 2011), with each season recycling American nightmare material: haunted houses, asylums, witches, freak shows, slasher hotels. Beneath the gore the show worries about identity and survival: essays here ask what demonic possession threatens in personal identity, whether death in the Murder House is really a harm, whether conjoined twins are one person or two, how to keep hold of reality in a gaslighting world, and why America itself keeps producing these stories.
115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and P: Iron Man and Captain America are Marvel's two flagship heroes, and their clash in the Civil War storyline over government registration of superhumans split fans down the middle. This book takes their quarrel seriously as a debate over American values: essays here ask who is the better hero and the better friend, whether Tony's failures or Steve's certainties embody virtue, whether humility is a moral achievement or herd instinct, and whether either man's answer to the freedom-versus-security dilemma can be right.
116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistanc: George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) is the defining dystopia: Big Brother watches everyone, Newspeak shrinks thought, and the Party rewrites history in Winston Smith's Oceania. Far from obsolete, it reads like tomorrow's news: essays here ask whether 'alternative facts' put us inside the novel already, why the proles never revolt, how media monopoly and weaponized language do the Party's work, whether the real enemies of freedom are states or corporations, and what kind of thinking could resist it.
